title: One more medicine, and the night it went wrong
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; no doses are given. Every start, stop and dose is the attending’s decision, taken from the label and your unit’s protocol.
intro:
You are the first-year nephrology fellow in the clinic of a tertiary hospital in Batangas. Mr. Alfredo “Fred” Domingo, 61, runs a sari-sari store in Lipa City. He has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension for 8, and chronic kidney disease (CKD) for 3. He takes losartan at the highest dose he tolerates, metformin, and a long-acting sulfonylurea. His body mass index is 28 kg/m².

His estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is 36 mL/min/1.73 m², his urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) 900 mg/g on two samples, potassium 4.8 mmol/L, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) 8.1%, standardized blood pressure 132/80 mm Hg. Twice this month he felt shaky and sweaty in the late morning, on days he skipped lunch to mind the store. His daughter says: “Doc, we can afford one more medicine every month, not three. Which one?”

n1.prompt: Which do you recommend to the attending?

choices.text: Finerenone, a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (nsMRA), since his albuminuria persists on a renin-angiotensin system inhibitor (RASi).
choices.feedback: He is a FIDELIO-DKD patient, and the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2024 guideline suggests an nsMRA here (2A). But few trial participants were on an SGLT2 inhibitor, his potassium is already 4.8, it is out of pocket, and the SGLT2 inhibitor carries the stronger recommendation.
choices.then: The attending chooses dapagliflozin first and keeps finerenone as the next step if his ACR stays high.

choices.text: Add an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor to his losartan for more albuminuria lowering.
choices.feedback: KDIGO recommends avoiding any combination of an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker and a direct renin inhibitor (1B). It adds hyperkalemia and kidney injury, not a new pathway.

choices.text: Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA), because it also helps his weight.
choices.feedback: FLOW showed real kidney benefit (number needed to treat [NNT] 20 over 3 years). But KDIGO places a GLP-1 RA after metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor for glucose (1B); it is an injection needing cold storage and is not on the PhilHealth list.

choices.text: A sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i): dapagliflozin, which is on the PhilHealth Guaranteed and Accessible Medications for Outpatient Treatment (GAMOT) list.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2024 recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor in type 2 diabetes with CKD at an eGFR of 20 or more (1A). In DAPA-CKD, 19 people treated for about 2.4 years prevented one major kidney or heart event; in CREDENCE, 22 over 2.5 years. Its benefit adds to his losartan, and he can sustain it every month.

n2.scene: His late-morning shaky spells happen on days he skips lunch. He is on full-dose metformin and the long-acting sulfonylurea.

choices.text: Increase the sulfonylurea to bring his HbA1c below 6.5%.
choices.feedback: As GFR falls, sulfonylureas are cleared more slowly and the kidney makes less glucose, so hypoglycemia becomes more likely. He is already having it. A target below 6.5% suits a younger patient with a low hypoglycemia risk.
choices.then: The attending sets a less strict target and reviews the sulfonylurea instead.

choices.text: Set his HbA1c target for him, toward the upper part of the below-6.5% to below-8.0% range given his hypoglycemia; review the long-acting sulfonylurea with the attending; reassess metformin at an eGFR below 45, with the dose from the label.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2022 recommends an individualized HbA1c target from below 6.5% to below 8.0% (1C). The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label says to reassess benefit and risk if eGFR falls below 45 in a patient already taking metformin, and KDIGO recommends metformin at an eGFR of 30 or more (1B).

choices.text: Stop metformin now: it is contraindicated below an eGFR of 45.
choices.feedback: The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) label sets the contraindication below 30. Between 30 and 45 it says do not start, and reassess if already taking. Stopping it now removes a useful drug and may push him toward more sulfonylurea.
choices.then: The attending keeps metformin, checks its dose against the label, and reviews the sulfonylurea.

choices.text: Keep both drugs as they are, and tell him never to skip lunch.
choices.feedback: Practical advice, but the drug problem remains: a long-acting sulfonylurea in falling GFR, and a metformin dose that needs checking at this eGFR.
choices.then: The attending reviews the sulfonylurea and checks the metformin dose against the label.

n3.prompt: What do you do and teach at the start?

choices.text: Start it, and tell him to stop it if his creatinine goes up at all.
choices.feedback: A small early eGFR dip is the drug lowering glomerular pressure, which is how it protects him. A “stop at any rise” rule throws away the benefit.
choices.then: You correct the instruction and teach the sick-day rule instead, with a recheck in a few weeks.

choices.text: Start it and recheck his laboratory tests in 6 months.
choices.feedback: Six months misses the window: creatinine and potassium should be rechecked within a few weeks, and he needs the sick-day rule before he leaves.
choices.then: You book a recheck in a few weeks and teach the sick-day rule.

choices.text: Review his volume status and any diuretic; teach genital hygiene and the sick-day rule (hold it during vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake, acute illness and before major surgery; restart when eating and drinking normally); warn that ketoacidosis can occur with near-normal glucose; recheck creatinine and potassium in a few weeks, expecting a small dip.
choices.feedback: These are the module’s start-up checks (the sick-day rule is a KDIGO practice point). In EMPA-KIDNEY ketoacidosis was rare, 6 versus 1 patients, but it can occur with near-normal glucose, so the family must know the warning signs.

n4.scene: His eGFR is 32, down from 36. Potassium is 4.9 mmol/L. He feels well, is eating and drinking normally, and has had no dizziness or shaky spells since the sulfonylurea was reviewed.
n4.prompt: What do you do about the eGFR?

choices.text: Continue the SGLT2 inhibitor. A small early dip is the expected pressure effect; recheck on the usual schedule.
choices.feedback: Both an SGLT2 inhibitor and a RASi lower glomerular pressure, so an early eGFR dip is a sign of the drug working, not of injury. KDIGO lets it continue even below an eGFR of 20 if tolerated (practice point).

choices.text: Continue it, but repeat the creatinine every week for a month.
choices.feedback: Continuing is right. Weekly tests in a well, eating patient add cost to a family paying out of pocket and do not change the plan.

choices.text: Stop it: his kidneys are getting worse.
choices.feedback: Stopping gives up the protection for an expected change. The dip is the pressure coming down; recheck it, and stop only if the rise is large or he is volume depleted.
choices.then: The attending restarts it and explains the dip to the family.

n5.scene: The emergency room resident calls you. Mr. Domingo has vomited since yesterday and has abdominal pain and fast, deep breathing. He kept taking all his medicines, including dapagliflozin and metformin, “because the doctor said every day.” His glucose is 190 mg/dL; his eGFR has fallen to 24.

choices.text: Hold the dapagliflozin, give an antiemetic and fluids, and send him home with a reminder of the sick-day rule.
choices.feedback: Holding it is right. But vomiting, abdominal pain and fast breathing on an SGLT2 inhibitor mean ketoacidosis must be excluded tonight, whatever the glucose.
choices.then: You call back and ask for a blood gas and ketones before he leaves: a metabolic acidosis with high ketones. He is admitted, and you call the attending.

choices.text: A glucose of 190 rules out ketoacidosis. Give fluids and an antiemetic, and continue his medicines.
choices.feedback: Ketoacidosis on an SGLT2 inhibitor can occur with near-normal glucose. Continuing it, and metformin, during vomiting breaks the sick-day rule.
choices.then: The emergency room resident checks a blood gas anyway: a metabolic acidosis with high ketones. You call the attending; he is admitted.

choices.text: Send him home on all his medicines with an antiemetic.
choices.feedback: He has the warning signs of ketoacidosis and a falling eGFR, and every medicine he is told to keep taking makes it worse tonight.
choices.then: The emergency room resident, uneasy, checks a blood gas: a metabolic acidosis with high ketones. You call the attending; he is admitted.

choices.text: Suspect SGLT2 inhibitor–associated ketoacidosis despite the near-normal glucose: hold dapagliflozin and metformin, ask for a blood gas and ketones, call the attending nephrologist now, and admit.
choices.feedback: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, fast breathing or drowsiness on an SGLT2 inhibitor, even with normal glucose, and a creatinine rise with vomiting are both on the module’s stop-and-call list. Vomiting also causes volume depletion and acute kidney injury.
choices.then: The blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis with high ketones. The attending admits him and treats him per the hospital protocol.

end.title: Three months later
end.text: He recovered, and his eGFR returned to 33. The attending reviewed with him and his daughter whether and when to restart dapagliflozin, and the sick-day rule is now written on a card in Tagalog taped to the store counter. His ACR is still above 30 mg/g with a normal potassium, so finerenone is the next step when the family can afford it. The chart says so: deferred for cost, not forgotten.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • When the family can buy one more medicine, choose the pillar with the best evidence for this patient that they can sustain: usually the SGLT2 inhibitor, on top of a RASi.
  • Quote the absolute benefit with the time: about 1 in 19 over 2.4 years in DAPA-CKD.
  • Set the HbA1c target for the person and watch for hypoglycemia as GFR falls; check metformin against the label at every eGFR change.
  • The early eGFR dip is the pressure coming down. Recheck it; do not stop for it.
  • Teach the sick-day rule at the start, and treat vomiting, abdominal pain or fast breathing on an SGLT2 inhibitor as possible ketoacidosis, even with near-normal glucose.

See Mechanism, The four pillars, Glucose and Access and cost.
